transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Ms. Nakamura, thank you for taking a moment to talk with me. I wanted to sit down and discuss something that happened with your care overnight.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Is everything okay? I was reading about post-op hypotension on this forum and my blood pressure felt really low around 3 AM.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I can see you're looking that up right now, and it's completely understandable that you're searching for answers. I want to be very honest with you about what happened. We failed to check your vital signs as often as we should have.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: What does that mean? I thought the monitors were automatic.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: The monitors track your heart rate, but we are required to manually check and record your blood pressure every hour after this specific procedure. For a period of two hours last night, those checks didn't happen. Because of that, we didn't realize your blood pressure had dropped until the next scheduled check.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Two hours? You missed two hours of checks?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: That is correct. Does that make sense so far, or can I clarify how the monitoring is supposed to work?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: It makes sense. It just... I felt so dizzy. I tried to press the call button but I was too tired. I felt like I was disappearing.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It sounds like you felt completely alone in that moment and terrified that something was happening to you while we weren't looking.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Exactly. I'm twenty-three. I'm not supposed to be in a state where I can't even call for help. Who forgot? Was it the nurse? Or you?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: There was a breakdown in the communication and the scheduling on the unit. The system for tracking the hourly checks wasn't followed.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: But who is responsible? I need to know why this happened.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: The team on the floor didn't maintain the protocol. It was a failure in the workflow of the ward.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: That's a very corporate way of saying you messed up. Are you sorry?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It is a very distressing situation to go through.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I'm not asking if it's distressing. I'm asking if you're apologizing.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I recognize that this is a frightening experience for you, especially for your first time in a hospital.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: My blood pressure was low for two hours. Did that do any permanent damage to my kidneys? I saw a paper about acute kidney injury.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I can see you're really worried about the long-term impact on your organs. It is incredibly scary to feel like your body is failing and the people meant to protect you aren't there.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Then what happens now? How do we know it won't happen again tonight?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We are going to keep a very close eye on you today.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: That's not a plan. How exactly are you keeping an eye on me?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We'll be monitoring your vitals.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Every hour? Like you were supposed to?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We will be checking them more frequently.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Is there a written order for that? Or is it just a verbal agreement?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We'll make sure the staff knows.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I don't feel safe. I feel like if I go to sleep, I'm just hoping someone remembers to check on me.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I can hear how much your trust has been shaken. It is a heavy thing to carry, feeling like you have to be your own advocate when you're this exhausted.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I'm a graduate student. I'm used to doing the work myself, but I can't monitor my own blood pressure while I'm unconscious.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: You're right. You shouldn't have to carry that burden.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: So what is the actual step-by-step for today?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We will continue with the standard post-op observations.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: The standard ones that were missed?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We'll be more diligent.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: That is so vague. When do I see the attending physician? I want them to explain the risk of the two-hour gap.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I'll see if they can stop by during rounds.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: When are rounds?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Usually in the morning.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: So I have to wait until maybe tomorrow?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We'll try to make it happen soon.

H.justification: The resident never interrupts the patient and remains calm and regulated despite repeated pushback and direct questioning.

E.justification: The error (failure to check vitals) is named in the second turn, lay language is used, and comprehension is checked ('Does that make sense so far?').

A.justification: The resident never uses direct apology language and deflects responsibility to 'a breakdown in communication' and 'the workflow of the ward' when asked who is responsible.

R.justification: The resident specifically names emotions ('terrified', 'frightening', 'shaken') and references the patient's specific experience of feeling alone.

T.justification: The resident provides only vague placeholders ('more frequently', 'we'll try to make it happen') without specific timelines, a named patient role, or a concrete prevention plan.
